newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Boots gains on loyalty card hopes.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Boots gains on loyalty card hopes.

text.p: Britain's biggest pharmacist Boots Co Plc on Wednesday joined the loyalty card stakes with the nationwide launch of its Advantage Card. The retailer's shares rose on hopes for a sales boost from the card, which is expected to break even this financial year and cover its costs by the end of the next year.

The card, available from September 1, will cost Boots 52 million pounds ($84.5 million) over three years, but is expected to deliver a four percent sales increase by the end of 1998/99. Boots The Chemists sales last year totalled 3.3 billion pounds.

Prospects of a sales uplift from the card and longer term benefits from mountain of data it will provide about individual customer's shopping habits helped push up Boots' shares. They stood 13.5 pence higher at 784.5 pence by 1353 GMT .
Retail analysts said although the initial cost was more than expected the data on the card's microchip technology would give Boots a significant advantage over competitors.

"Previously information was driven by product and transaction now it will be customer behaviour," said Robert Miller, retail analyst at Dresdner Kleinwort Benson. " It's pretty potent information," he said.
Boots' card follows other retailers' loyalty programmes, including three of Britain's big four food superstores, including Tesco Plc and J. Sainsbury Plc.
Tesco's Clubcard, the first of these schemes launched in 1995, helped the retailer steal market leadership from rival Sainsbury.
Director of Boots beauty business Steve Hill told a news conference the microchip would give Boots access to highly detailed information about its customers.
He said the company would be able to look at its business customer by customer and could offer shoppers personalised promotions based on what they have bought in the past.
He said the card had scope for a whole range of additional functions, including medical, health insurance, or social security.
Boots The Chemist managing director Steve Russell predicted the card would be even more important for Boots than the introduction of electronic point of sale technology.
"In driving a step change in performance the Advantage Card could be even more important," he said.
Other retail analysts said Boots was one of the few non-food retailers with the customer flow to make a loyalty scheme worthwhile.
Richard Perks at retail consultants Verdict said Boots also had the technical back up to make use of the information gathered via the card.
"It will give them much more control over their business, it's potentially hugely powerful information," he said.

Customers signing up for the Boots card will receive one point worth one pence, for every 25 pence spent in Boots The Chemists. The points can be redeemed against a range of 10,000 health and beauty products and services sold by the company.
Boots expects more than eight million of its customers to sign up to the card by September 1998 based on two regional trials running since October 1995.
Russell said Boots believed the loyalty card could raise the average amount spent in Boots by about one third.

He said the average transaction was currently 6.11 pounds, but trials in East Anglia and the south west of England showed the card did increase shoppers' average spending when they visited the store. "I think the average spend on the Advantage card is about 30 percent higher," he told Reuters by telephone.

Phil Douty, head of customer communications, estimated the sales boost would translate into gross profit of 109 million pounds. "Over the three-year period the gross profit accruing from the incremental sales is 109 million pounds.....before all the expenses," he said.

The investment in marketing, database, and training will be 25 million pounds this year, falling to 14 million next year and 13 million in 1999/2000. --London Newsroom + 44 171 542 7717 ($ = 0.615 British
Pounds)
